title: Choosing a model

kcs.statement: Choose an embedding model by language and domain, max input, dimensions and cost.
Decide with an eval on your own queries, not a leaderboard alone.
Respect query and document prefixes, and never mix models in one index.

visual_fit.why: A checklist of model properties; the comparison table of reference models already sets the options side by side.

misconceptions.statement: More dimensions always means better retrieval.

glossary.md: Massive Text Embedding Benchmark (Muennighoff et al., 2022): a public leaderboard of embedding models across many tasks.

md: There are hundreds of embedding models. Choose using questions about **your** data, not a leaderboard rank:

1. **Language and domain.** English only? Multilingual? Legal, medical or code?
2. **Input length.** Do your chunks fit the model's maximum?
3. **Dimensions.** More dimensions means more memory and slower search. It doesn't automatically mean better results.
4. **Cost and hosting.** A paid API (per token) or open weights you run yourself (GPU/CPU cost, data stays in-house).
5. **Quality on your own queries.** Use a benchmark like [[MTEB]] (Muennighoff et al., 2022) to shortlist, then evaluate on 50–200 labelled queries from your real traffic. Benchmark rank and rank on your data often differ.

block.title: A few reference points (check current docs before deciding)
rows: Small, fast, English, open weights (Apache-2.0). A good baseline.
Open weights. Expect query/passage prefixes or an instruction (see below).
API. About \$0.13 per 1M tokens. Higher MTEB score.

block.md: Some models are trained **asymmetrically** and expect markers. E5 models want `"query: "` in front of queries and `"passage: "` in front of documents. BGE recommends an instruction prefix for short queries. Forget the prefix and quality drops, with no error to tell you.
block.title: Prefixes are part of the model

block.md: Some models are trained **Matryoshka-style** (Kusupati et al., 2022), so the first $m$ dimensions are themselves a usable embedding. OpenAI exposes this through the `dimensions` parameter. Its docs note that `text-embedding-3-large` shortened to 256 dimensions still beats the older `text-embedding-ada-002` at 1,536 on MTEB. If you truncate vectors yourself, **re-normalize** afterwards.
block.title: Shorter vectors, almost free

question.prompt_md: Your index holds 2M chunks embedded with `text-embedding-3-small`. You want better quality from `text-embedding-3-large`. What must you do?

options.md: Re-embed all 2M chunks with the new model and query that new index with the new model
options.why_md: Right. New model, new space. The usual pattern is to build the new index alongside the old one, evaluate it, then switch over (see Real world: model migration).

options.md: Embed only new queries with the large model
options.why_md: Queries and documents would then live in different spaces, and scores would be meaningless.

options.md: Truncate the large model's 3,072 dims to 1,536 so they fit the old index
options.why_md: Matching sizes doesn't make the spaces compatible.

question.prompt_md: Which of these should drive your choice of embedding model? Select all that apply.

options.md: Retrieval quality measured on your own labelled queries
options.why_md: Yes. It's the strongest signal you can get.

options.md: Whether your chunks fit within its max input length
options.why_md: Yes. Otherwise text gets truncated or rejected.
No. More dimensions cost memory and speed and don't guarantee better results.
Yes. A model never trained on your language or jargon will struggle.

recap.pitfall: A leaderboard winner can lose on your queries; and a new model means re-embedding everything.
